questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Limit of an Inverse Trigonometric Function at a Point
questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/fc06a4e63f38a315dd3944f65f871cca2dbdddee26ec268e857f79e5f4ab8848.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)$ is $x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$  

Now, substituting $x=1$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}{\pi x} & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)}{\pi \cdot (1)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\pi }{4})}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

The domain of $\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)$ is $x\in [-1,1].$  

Now, substituting $x=0$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,0}(2x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)) & =2\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(0) \\  & =2\cdot 0\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The domain of $\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x)$ is $x\in [-1,1].$   

Now, substituting $x=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ directly into the limit, we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\sqrt{3}/2}(2\sqrt{3}x+6\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x)) & =2\sqrt{3}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})+6\cdot \operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =3+6\cdot (\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =3+\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2+2x)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ Moreover, from the graph, we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2+2x)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2+2x)=3\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})=-\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

First, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6-x):$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/04dd8257ef32291b930aa29f5bed4de2c41761692fd48d08ed2479f6cbd78659.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6-x)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ Moreover, from the graph, we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6-x)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\frac{7}{\pi }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(6-x))=\frac{7}{\pi }\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})=-\frac{7}{2}.
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,\infty }8\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})$ is undefined.

First, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x+1):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/e441953c2cefc6f817a64cb7ce0ebce53164ebb4d3974ae871b14d57450b5167.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x+1)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ Moreover, from the graph, we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x+1)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }(\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x+1))=\pi -(-\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{3\pi }{2}.

First, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x+3):$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/bb49c052cabe12e8869270ab61b1de9e7f45b6acd6eaa9bc0d4c6892446a7cb6.png)

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x+3)=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }(10\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x+3))=(10\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})=5\pi .
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Limit Involving Trigonometric Functions and Their Inverses
questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/ca5e8035505f20619b6707d6d1f2d0b7b2f125a004a0dbd9d448840b0e4ffd99.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)$ is $x\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$  

As $x$ increases to $\infty ,$ the graph tends to $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/f5cef3bda76e80edfa467a90823c9b6ad6aca1f8a5e8e3e06dc585258e975e0a.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+1)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$  

As $x$ increases to $\infty ,$ the graph tends to $y=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+1)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y=\arccos(x){:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/9dcc5a116c2a564547283783a7df7b1cd3a9ab3b76ac24dc2695c4cb367796d5.png)

The domain of $\arccos(x)$ is $x \in [-1,1].$  

Now, substituting $x=0$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x)-\pi }{x-\pi }) & =\frac{\operatorname{arccos}⁡(0)-\pi }{0-\pi } \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\pi }{2}-\pi )}{(-\pi )} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{\pi }{2})}{(-\pi )} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's sketch the graph of $y = \arccos(x-1){:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/4ccf7e79e19f49027f615a075e655139e6926b3ba30fe35d63078fd7917d8869.png)

The domain of $\arccos(x-1)$ is $x \in [0,2].$ This means that $\arccos(x-1)$ is undefined outside this interval.

Therefore, $\lim_\limits{x \to \, \infty} \arccos(x-1)$ is undefined.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13996467/assets/06d01e3eb47f69e5172e0ba3c99708a05c79b12a48764fe29c50e94f93b73dd1.png)

The domain of   $\arctan \left(2x+1 \right)$ is $(-\infty,\infty).$   

As $x$ increases to $\infty,$ the graph tends to $y={\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}{2}}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x+1)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
